## Abstract {.unnumbered}

After the M7.5 earthquake that struck coastal Venezuela on 24 June 2026, at least eight
organisations released satellite-derived building-damage products. We evaluated the six
that published an analysed extent against three references with complementary blind
spots: expert damage points (Copernicus EMS), a crowd review of AI-flagged locations
(MapSwipe), and 415 field reports (ChatMap).

No product supports acting on a single flagged building: precision ran 0.05–0.09 even
in each product's most favourable region, and although the expert reference misses
lesser damage, the most generous defensible reading still leaves every product below
0.28. The products do rank neighbourhoods well enough to triage, within a damage zone
that is already identified. The practical way to use them is to count agreement between
independent products. Flagging buildings at the better agreement thresholds roughly doubles the building-level performance (F1) of any single product, the count out-ranks every single product at ranking neighbourhoods (at both cell sizes tested), and it needs no weights, training data or reference, so it can be computed as soon as the second product arrives.


## The event, the products, and the references

An M7.5 earthquake, preceded about 40 seconds earlier by an M7.2, struck near Yumare on
the Venezuelan coast at 22:05 UTC on 24 June 2026. Severe damage was concentrated along
the La Guaira coastal strip, in western Caracas, and in several inland towns. Copernicus
EMS rapid mapping was activated the same night (EMSR884). Products came from a variety
of organisations: the EU's rapid-mapping service (Copernicus Emergency Management
Service, CEMS), a technology company (Microsoft AI for Good), universities (Oregon State
University, working with NASA; the University of Houston), an NGO (IMPACT Initiatives),
UN bodies (the United Nations Environment Programme / Office for the Coordination of
Humanitarian Affairs (UNEP/OCHA) Joint Environment Unit; the World Food Programme,
working with the Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology (LIST) and the European
Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN)), a volunteer AI platform (the Humanitarian
OpenStreetMap Team's fAIr), and DISHA (Data Insights for Social and Humanitarian
Action), an initiative of UN Global Pulse. These products disagree with each other,
sometimes by a wide margin. A coordinator of search-and-rescue (SAR) teams receiving
several of them in the same week has no established way to decide which to trust, for
what purpose, and at what spatial scale.

We evaluate the six products that published a defined or defensible analysed extent,
the area the product actually examined (@tbl-products): without one, "no flag" cannot
be distinguished from "never looked", so neither misses nor false alarms can be counted
fairly. Throughout, a *flag* is a building a product marked as damaged to any extent.

| Product | Provider | Sensing basis | Analysed buildings | Damage flags* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft AI4G | Microsoft | VHR optical + AI classifier | 72,162 (Overture footprints) | 8,410 |
| IMPACT v2 | IMPACT Initiatives | Sentinel-1 radar coherence change | swath (~372 km²) | 22,954 |
| OSU | Oregon State Univ. / NASA | Sentinel-1 radar coherence change | swath (~471 km²) | 31,259 |
| UH QuakeDamage | Univ. of Houston | VHR optical (Vantor imagery, author-confirmed) + AI classifier grading every footprint | 447,263 incl. intact | ~91k dmg/destroyed |
| LIST | WFP / LIST / CERN | AI change detection on before/after radar imagery (provider-stated) | 163,225 | 15,904 in core region |
| UNEP debris | UNEP/OCHA JEU | Sentinel-1 radar change detection on building footprints (debris tonnage modeled from the detected damage) | no extent (stated assumption) | 96,046 |

: Products evaluated. *Flag counts are as mapped onto the shared building-footprint
base used throughout; totals differ from providers' native counts because of
footprint-base differences. OSU figures refer to its v0 delivery, the version available
during the response. {#tbl-products}

![Who analysed where. Each product's analysed extent, the five expert-mapped CEMS AOIs
(dashed black), and, in red with the zoom frame below, the ~61 km² core region where the
head-to-head and combination analyses live. UH publishes no extent (its polygon is
derived from its own classified footprints); UNEP publishes none at all and is scored
under a stated coverage
assumption.](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/fig_extents_map.png){#fig-extents}

We use two reporting regions throughout. *As delivered* scores each product across
everything it shipped, wherever the expert reference mapped. This is the view that
matches what responders actually received. The *core region* is the ~61 km² where all six products
and the reference overlap: one shared area on which every predictor is scored alike, and each product's favourable case (it holds 96% of the expert-recorded
damage). Sections and captions state which region they use.

Each of the three references sees something different. Copernicus EMS provides trained-analyst
damage points and is the primary reference: every headline precision and recall is
computed against it, under one matching rule (a building counts as damaged if a CEMS
point lies within 10 m). MapSwipe is a crowd campaign in which more than 400 volunteers
reviewed ~50 m cells at locations AI products had flagged. It can refute a false alarm
but can never reveal a miss, so it adjudicates disputed flags and is never used as
ground truth. ChatMap is 415 building-level damage reports from field teams,
positives-only with no survey frame. It can reveal misses but says nothing about false
alarms (@fig-refarch). Because their blind spots do not overlap, the three check one
another. One consequence applies to every number here: against an incomplete reference,
measured precision is a lower bound and measured recall an upper bound.

![The three reference datasets at a glance. Two are HOT-run and easily confused:
MapSwipe is remote volunteers voting on ~50 m cells, used to adjudicate false alarms;
ChatMap is field teams reporting building-level points from the ground, used to reveal
misses.](artefacts/RQ0-matching-basis/figs/reference_architecture.png){#fig-refarch}

available [here](https://ocha-dap.github.io/ds-geospatial-impact-estimates/manuscript/)
with a passphrase shared separately; it contains the geography benchmark and all sensitivity analyses in full.)

## No product supports acting on a single flagged building {#sec-flags}

Building-level precision was low for every product. As delivered, precision across
everything the expert reference mapped ran from 0.009 (UH) to 0.081 (Microsoft). Even
in the core region, where every product scores best, precision reached only 0.045–0.093
against recall of 0.31–0.69: ten to twenty false alarms for every hit, in the products' best
case. The products do find damage; what they also produce is an enormous number of
flags with no reference record of damage underneath them. At this task a simple model of building
density and terrain performs in the same range ([the geography
benchmark](#app-null-brief)), so single-product flags should be treated as weak
evidence on their own.

The gap between the two frames is itself a finding. Core-region numbers are each
product's favourable case; as delivered, the same product can be several times weaker
(UH: 0.093 in the core against 0.009 across its delivery), because precision falls by
roughly the share of a product's flags placed in areas with little recorded damage
(@fig-peraoi). What a provider chooses to ship matters about as much as how well its
model detects: the product that shipped only its best-covered strip kept most of its
core-region precision as delivered, while products that shipped broad extents lowered
theirs.

![**Region: each CEMS AOI separately, plus the pooled as-delivered total.** Per-AOI
scorecard. Left: precision lower bound per product per CEMS AOI; right: recall where
the reference is thick enough to support it. 96% of all CEMS damage points are in the
first column; outside it, measured precision (0.00–0.02) cannot separate product
over-flagging from reference
incompleteness.](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2i_per_aoi_scorecard.png){#fig-peraoi}

The expert reference is itself incomplete, and this was measured rather than assumed.
ChatMap, the one reference collected on the ground independently of any satellite
imagery, audits the expert map: CEMS captured 94% of field-reported destroyed buildings
but only 49% of those significantly damaged (@fig-gradeslope). The individual products
share the same slope: everything sees destruction better than damage. Some damage was missed by everything: about 11% of field-reported damage points, mostly in inland hill
communities, had no flag from any product within 20 m despite lying inside analysed
extents. Recall was never the products' weakness; precision is the limiting factor.

![**Region: within the CEMS-analysed extents; reference: field reports (20 m GPS tolerance).** Recall by damage grade. Each line is one dataset's recall against
field-reported damage, at "complete" destruction versus "significant" damage. Every
line slopes down: the products and the expert reference alike find lighter damage far
less often, which is why measured recall is an upper bound and measured precision a
lower bound.](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2e_grade_slope.png){#fig-gradeslope}

Because the reference misses lesser damage, the headline precisions are lower bounds,
and there is more than one defensible way to define the reference. @fig-bounds shows
what happens as the grading criteria are loosened using the other reference data this
study collected: first adding the points CEMS graded *possibly damaged*, then instead
crediting the flags the MapSwipe crowd reviewed and confirmed as damaged, and finally
both together. The result is a range of possible precision values per product, with a
realistic upper bound at the top. Even at the upper bound every product stays below
0.28. The poor-precision conclusion is not an artefact of the strict reference choice.

![**Region: core (61 km²).** Each product's precision under four reference definitions,
flags fixed. Filled brown dot: the expert points graded *Damaged* or *Destroyed*, the
paper's reference and the lower bound. Open circle: also counting the points graded
*possibly damaged* (labelled values). Open square: instead also counting the flags the
MapSwipe crowd reviewed and confirmed as damaged. Filled diamond: counting both
additions, the upper bound. A flag is credited only where volunteers actually reviewed its location and judged it damaged; unreviewed locations receive no credit, so
products the crowd barely saw (UH: 27%) have understated upper
bounds.](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2r_bounds_ladder.png){#fig-bounds}

## The products rank neighbourhoods well enough to triage, within the damage zone {#sec-ranking}

Asked which *neighbourhoods* to go to first, rather than which buildings, the products
do much better. In the core region, zoomed to the area already known to be damaged,
every product orders ~0.74 km² cells against the expert ordering at rank correlations
of 0.48–0.74, and the best products correctly identify most of the twenty worst-hit cells. The qualifier matters: scored across everything each product delivered, the correlations spread from −0.09 to 0.59 at the ~5 km² cell scale (@fig-ranktests), and
the ranking
task largely reduces to "find the damage zone", which coarse geography solves
almost by definition; the products' real ranking information is about where to go first
*within* a zone. Ranking is useful once the response has already narrowed to a known
damage area; it is not a way to find that area.

![**Regions: as delivered (left), core (right).** Each product's ranking of areas by
damage, compared with the expert ordering (Spearman rank correlation; higher = ranks
the worst-hit areas better). As delivered, rankings spread widely and one product's is
negative; restricted to the known damage zone, every product ranks usefully. This is
the basis for the caveat repeated throughout the paper: trust the neighbourhood ranking
*within* an identified damage zone, not for finding
one.](artefacts/RQ3-prioritization-error-structure/figs/rq3f_null_ranking_both_summary.png){#fig-ranktests}

Counting agreement between products improves that ranking (@fig-agreerank). Ranking
cells by their count of buildings with three or four products agreeing beats every
single product's ordering (ρ 0.78 against the best single's 0.74 at ~0.74 km² cells),
and for a shortlist, "which 20 cells first", high agreement is clearly better:
five-of-six agreement shortlists 16 of the 20 worst-hit cells against the best single
product's 13, and 10 against 4 at the finer scale.

![**Region: core (61 km²), both cell scales.** The six k-of-6 agreement rules at the area-ranking task, against each single product (grey). Top row: rank correlation with
the expert ordering over all cells. Bottom row: share of the 20 worst-hit cells that
make the predictor's own top-20 shortlist (tie-aware expected
value).](artefacts/RQ3-prioritization-error-structure/figs/rq3h_agreement_ranking_summary.png){#fig-agreerank}

## Count agreement between products {#sec-dial}

The products' errors fall in different places, so the number of them agreeing on a building
works as a threshold a responder can set. Flag every building any product marked and 97% of
known damage is covered, but a field team following those flags would make 26 site
visits for each damaged building it reached; require all six to agree and 93% of flags
are correct but only 18% of the damage is covered. Between the extremes, each added
agreeing product raises the odds that a flag is real, and setting the threshold fixes
the size of the field job the same day (@tbl-dial). Setting the threshold fixes how
many buildings field teams will visit; it does not fix how many of them will turn out
damaged.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-dial
#| tbl-cap: "Building-level performance of the six products and the six agreement rules in the core region, at matching radii of 10, 20, and 30 m. At 10 m, product cells also show the as-delivered value in parentheses; agreement rules are defined on the shared footprint base and exist only in the core region. Crowd-adjusted precision re-judges the expert-unmatched flags against the crowd verdicts (10 m); flags in cells the crowd never reviewed are assumed to contain damage at the same rate as the reviewed ones. Visits/find is field visits per damage point reached at 30 m, the finding distance; computed as flags ÷ R₃₀ × 1,467 reference points. Shading ranks values within each column (darker = higher; for visits/find, fewer)."
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT, style, loc
from matplotlib import colormaps
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex

five = {r: pd.read_csv(f"artefacts/RQ5-ensemble/rq5b_six_member{'' if r == 10 else f'_r{r}'}.csv").set_index("rule")
        for r in (10, 20, 30)}
asd = pd.read_csv("artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/rq2i_per_aoi_scorecard.csv")
asd = asd[asd.aoi == "ALL (as delivered)"].drop_duplicates("product").set_index("product")

products = ["MS", "IMPACT", "OSU", "UH", "LIST", "UNEP"]
rules = [f"{k}-of-6" for k in range(1, 7)]
labels = {"MS": "Microsoft", "IMPACT": "IMPACT v2"}
N_CEMS = 1467

disp, nums = [], []
for key in products + rules:
    d = {"rule": labels.get(key, key),
         "group": "Products" if key in products else "Voting rules (k of 6 agree)"}
    n = {}
    d["flags"] = f"{int(five[10].loc[key]['flagged']):,}"
    for r in (10, 20, 30):
        row = five[r].loc[key]
        for m, ml in (("P_cems", "P"), ("R_cems", "R"), ("F1_cems", "F1")):
            col = f"{ml}{r}"
            n[col] = float(row[m])
            if r == 10 and key in products and m in ("P_cems", "R_cems"):
                d[col] = f"{row[m]:.3f} ({float(asd.loc[key][m]):.3f})"
            else:
                d[col] = f"{row[m]:.3f}"
    n["Padj"] = float(five[10].loc[key]["P_crowd_adj"])
    d["Padj"] = f"{n['Padj']:.3f}"
    visits = five[10].loc[key]["flagged"] / (five[30].loc[key]["R_cems"] * N_CEMS)
    n["visits"] = -visits
    d["visits"] = f"{visits:.1f}"
    disp.append(d); nums.append(n)

cols = ["rule", "flags", "P10", "R10", "F110", "Padj",
        "P20", "R20", "F120", "P30", "R30", "F130", "visits"]
df = pd.DataFrame(disp)[["group"] + cols]
nm = pd.DataFrame(nums)[[c for c in cols if c not in ("rule", "flags")]]

cmap = colormaps["Blues"]
gt = (GT(df, rowname_col="rule", groupname_col="group")
      .tab_spanner("10 m", ["P10", "R10", "F110", "Padj"])
      .tab_spanner("20 m", ["P20", "R20", "F120"])
      .tab_spanner("30 m", ["P30", "R30", "F130", "visits"])
      .cols_label(flags="flags", P10="P", R10="R", F110="F1", Padj="P (crowd-adj)",
                  P20="P", R20="R", F120="F1", P30="P", R30="R", F130="F1",
                  visits="visits/find")
      .tab_options(column_labels_font_weight="bold",
                   row_group_font_weight="bold",
                   table_font_size="13px",
                   data_row_padding="4px"))
for col in nm.columns:
    vals = nm[col]
    lo, hi = vals.min(), vals.max()
    for i, v in enumerate(vals):
        t = 0.0 if hi == lo else (v - lo) / (hi - lo)
        gt = gt.tab_style(style.fill(color=to_hex(cmap(0.15 + 0.55 * t))),
                          loc.body(columns=[col], rows=[i]))
gt
```

Weight the count toward *independent methods*: products that share a sensing method
err together, and their agreement added the least information in our tests, while
products with nothing in common but the event cover for each other's blind spots
(@fig-frontier).

![**Region: core (61 km²).** The fifteen two-product rules. Pairing across independent methods lifts precision;
the pair sharing its entire method adds the
least.](artefacts/RQ5-ensemble/figs/rq5b_frontier_r10.png){#fig-frontier}

Counting agreement is also close to the ceiling of what any combination can achieve. A
statistically fitted combination of the six products scores about 18% higher on F1, but
fitting it requires the damage map a responder is still waiting for, so it explains the
event afterwards and cannot run during one; flat counting can be done as soon as the
second product arrives (@fig-bestf1).

![**Regions: core (left), as delivered (right).** Comparing performance measurements of
all products against each other and the derived combined products. Bar length and bar
label show F1, followed by precision and recall. The derived combined products (green)
are shown at their optimal performance weighting/configuration; they are defined on the
shared building base, so they exist only in the core
region.](artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/figs/rq8_best_f1_r10_summary.png){#fig-bestf1}

## Recommendations

::: {.callout-tip title="For responders"}
These recommendations are part of an ongoing dialogue with responders about what is
operationally most useful, and the clearest message so far concerns the first 72 hours,
when the pressing need is to narrow down the worst-hit areas. No single
product supports acting on individual flagged
buildings. The neighbourhood ranking can be trusted, but only *within* a damage zone
that is already identified: scored across everything a product delivered, its ranking
adds little to what coarse geography already encodes, while within the known damage
zone the products contain real information about where to go first (@sec-ranking).

Combining them works better. Counting agreement between products outperformed
every single product both at ranking neighbourhoods (@fig-agreerank) and at
flagging individual buildings, where the better agreement thresholds roughly doubled the F1 of any product alone (0.26–0.28 against the best single product's 0.15; @tbl-dial). So do not spend time choosing a product; spend it counting agreement between
products. Unlike a fitted model, counting requires no weights, no training data
and no reference, so it can be done as soon as the second product arrives. Weight the
count toward products with independent sensing methods, for the reason given in
@sec-dial.

That combination is also the most promising basis for a derived product usable at
building level. Which agreement threshold to act on depends on the precision-recall
trade a response is willing to make; @tbl-dial gives the flag counts and visit costs at
each level, and the choice is a workload, not a guaranteed hit rate. Nothing currently available sees lighter damage reliably, so plan shelter
assessments accordingly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="For providers"}
Publish an analysed extent; without one, a user cannot tell "no flag" from "not
analysed", so the product cannot be fairly evaluated or confidently used.
Publish per-building acquisition metadata (scene count and dates); those fields are what made it possible to trace one failure in this event to a single satellite scene. Where a
second scene confirms a flag, present that as an explicit confidence level. For the one
product whose metadata allowed the check, two-scene flags were 2.5 times more precise
than single-scene ones. Products should be validated in the kinds of places they are
deployed; the scene at issue here was the one absent from the provider's validation
set. And accept feedback during the activation: a crowd campaign
rejected 71% of one zone's flags within days, and there was no mechanism for returning that
result to the provider while reprocessing could still help.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="For evaluators and coordinators"}
A single expert reference understates precision most where damage is lighter. Publish
measured precision as a lower bound, or better, adjudicate the disputed flags against a
second reference and publish the interval. Unanimous product agreement without
expert corroboration turned out to be mostly real damage, so consensus doubles as a
detector of reference gaps and a field-validation queue. Finally, coverage is a
problem no provider can see alone: the inland communities missed by every product were
inside analysed extents, and nobody knew that nobody was seeing them. Maintaining a shared, live picture of who is looking where costs providers nothing and fixes the one problem here
that combining products cannot. In practice this points to four coordination functions:
a web viewer showing who detected what, where; an interpretation layer that
turns the combined products into the neighbourhood ranking and building-level
composites responders can act on; a consolidation space that receives raw deliveries,
with the coordinator supplying the template (analysed extent, metadata, a common
basemap and footprint set); and raw-imagery access for field teams with the
capacity to run their own analysis or manual mapping.
:::

## Limitations

This is one event, one geography, and mostly one damage zone: a single earthquake
in a coastal, dense-urban setting, and the core comparison region is only ~61 km², with
96% of the expert reference in a single AOI (Caraballeda). The specific rule orderings
and magnitudes are hypotheses elsewhere until replicated.

The references have limits of their own. The crowd campaign was seeded from two AI
products' flags, so it scrutinises products unevenly and can never see any product's
misses; the field reports are undated, positives-only, skewed toward destruction, and
come with no defined collection area.

What we know about the products is uneven. Input-imagery details and release dates
for several products await provider confirmation, and agreement rules inherit the
shared footprint base, so strict-agreement recall is understated.

The full statements of these limits, the sensitivity analyses behind every number, and
the geography benchmark are in the frozen technical record (manuscript v3).

### The two reporting regions {#app-regions .unnumbered}

Results are reported in one of two *regions*, and numbers are comparable only within
one:

| reporting region | what it is | used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Core region** | the ~61 km² intersection of the CEMS extents with all five extent-publishing products (@fig-extents): one shared cell set | voting, the pairwise rules, fusion, and the best-F1 geography comparison |
| **As delivered** | each product's full delivered footprint, wherever CEMS mapped: a different region per product | the as-delivered scorecard and geography benchmark; ranking test 1 |

: The two reporting regions. Sections and captions state which they use. The core
region gives every predictor an identical cell set (one geography score); as-delivered
is per-product by design, so the geography model is re-scored on each product's own
footprint there. {#tbl-regions}

Why the core region is so small, and what its numbers mean: the five extent-publishing
products mutually overlap over only ~100 km², with Microsoft's 210 km² strip the
binding constraint (UNEP publishes no extent and is treated as covering the region, the
same stated assumption as everywhere else). Intersecting with the expert reference then
trims the shared, scoreable area to ~61 km². The trim scores every predictor on the same area, at the cost of representativeness: the core region covers the most heavily damaged area, where the reference is densest and every product scores best, so
core-region numbers are each product's favourable case, while the as-delivered numbers
describe what a responder actually had (@sec-flags).

The same arithmetic is why DISHA is not a member. Its delivery included an analysed
extent (133.6 km², north-west Caracas and the La Guaira–Catia strip), but that extent
covers only 48% of the core region (29.3 of 60.8 km²) and holds 886 of the 1,467
expert damage points there. Admitting it would have halved the area on which all
products are compared and dropped 40% of the reference from every shared analysis, weakening the evaluation of the six other products; it therefore appears in the availability
inventory only.

### Matching products to references, in full {#app-matching .unnumbered}

The product and reference use different geometries (CEMS drops points on damaged
buildings, while each product flags its own footprints on its own building base), so there
is no shared list of instances on which to build a single confusion matrix. We therefore
score by *proximity*, a standard approach for detection-style evaluation: precision
anchors on the product (of its flagged buildings, how many have a CEMS damage point within
radius r?), and recall anchors on the reference (of the CEMS damage points, how many have a
product flag within r?). Each metric has its own denominator. Because the two metrics
are precision and recall, neither uses the undamaged background (true negatives), so the
size of that set affects no score.

False positives are classified under the standard scheme for detection
evaluation. Within the analysed extent the reference is treated as complete: a flag
with no reference record within the matching radius is a false positive, reference
damage with no flag is a miss, and the remaining buildings are, under the scheme, true
negatives (precision and recall never use that count, so it affects no headline
number). The rule is applied uniformly, so no product is advantaged by it. What this
paper adds is that the completeness assumption is tested rather than assumed:
the field reports measure the expert reference's own recall, every measured precision is
reported as a lower bound, and the expert-unmatched flags are re-judged against the
crowd (@sec-flags).

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Dual-anchored matching. Left: a product is scored only where it AND the reference both looked. Middle: recall anchors on the reference; for each CEMS damage point, the question is whether a product flag lies within radius r. Right: precision anchors on the product; for each flagged building, whether a CEMS point lies within r. Each metric has its own denominator."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mp
import numpy as np
from shapely.geometry import Point

R = 0.16
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 5.1))
a0 = ax[0]
c1, c2 = Point(-0.28, 0).buffer(0.75), Point(0.28, 0).buffer(0.75)
inter = c1.intersection(c2)
a0.add_patch(mp.Polygon(np.asarray(inter.exterior.coords), closed=True, fc="#c8e6c9", ec="none"))
for c, col, lab, xy in ((c1, "tab:blue", "CEMS analysed extent", (-0.75, 0.62)),
                        (c2, "tab:orange", "product AOI", (0.42, 0.62))):
    a0.add_patch(mp.Polygon(np.asarray(c.exterior.coords), closed=True, fc="none", ec=col, lw=2))
    a0.annotate(lab, xy, fontsize=9, color=col)
a0.annotate("scored HERE only", (0, -0.05), fontsize=10, ha="center", weight="bold", color="#2e7d32")
a0.set_title("1 · where scoring happens", fontsize=10)
a1 = ax[1]
for x, y in [(-0.38, 0.22), (0.05, -0.32), (-0.6, -0.5), (0.62, -0.15)]:
    a1.scatter(x, y, marker="s", s=70, c="tab:orange", zorder=3)
for x, y, hit in [(-0.45, 0.3, True), (0.15, -0.25, True), (0.45, 0.42, False)]:
    a1.add_patch(mp.Circle((x, y), R, fc="none", ec="grey", ls="--"))
    a1.scatter(x, y, marker="*", s=180, c="k", zorder=4)
    a1.annotate("TP" if hit else "FN (missed)", (x + 0.05, y + 0.13), fontsize=9,
                color="#2e7d32" if hit else "#c62828", weight="bold")
a1.set_title("2 · RECALL — anchor on each CEMS point", fontsize=10)
a2 = ax[2]
for x, y in [(-0.36, 0.25), (0.2, -0.14)]:
    a2.scatter(x, y, marker="*", s=180, c="k", zorder=4)
for x, y, hit in [(-0.45, 0.32, True), (0.1, -0.2, True), (0.5, 0.45, False), (-0.15, -0.6, False)]:
    a2.add_patch(mp.Circle((x, y), R, fc="none", ec="grey", ls="--"))
    a2.scatter(x, y, marker="s", s=70, c="tab:orange", zorder=3)
    a2.annotate("TP" if hit else "FP (false alarm)", (x + 0.05, y + 0.13), fontsize=9,
                color="#2e7d32" if hit else "#c62828", weight="bold")
a2.set_title("3 · PRECISION — anchor on each product flag", fontsize=10)
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlim(-1.05, 1.05); a.set_ylim(-1.0, 0.9)
    a.set_aspect("equal"); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
h = [plt.Line2D([], [], marker="*", ls="", ms=13, c="k", label="CEMS damage point"),
     plt.Line2D([], [], marker="s", ls="", ms=8, c="tab:orange", label="product-flagged building"),
     plt.Line2D([], [], ls="--", c="grey", label="match radius r")]
fig.legend(handles=h, loc="lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 0.97))
```
